answer.answer:
The court is a rectangle marked out with lines 40 mm wide (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 1.1).
A shuttle landing on a line is in, not out: all the lines form part of the area which they define (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 1.3), and it is a fault only if the shuttle lands outside the boundaries of the court, i.e. not on or within the boundary lines (Clause 13.3.1). When the shuttle lands in, the Line Judge says nothing but points to the line with the right hand while looking towards the Umpire (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.4); no 'Out' call is made.
For contrast, the 'Out' call is made only when the shuttle lands out — the Line Judge calls 'Out' promptly with both arms extended horizontally (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 8.3) — and a Line Judge does not call or signal until the shuttle has touched the floor or anything outside the court boundaries (Clause 8.6), which confirms a shuttle touching a line (part of the court) is not called out.

Under Law 13.4 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26), it is a fault if, in play, a player invades an opponent's court over the net with racket or person — except that the striker may follow the shuttle over the net with the racket in the course of a stroke after the initial point of contact with the shuttle is on the striker's side of the net. Law 10.2.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) says that in a rally the shuttle may be hit by the server and receiver alternately from any position on that player's side of the net until the shuttle ceases to be in play — i.e. normal play keeps each player on their own side, with the only over-the-net racket allowance being the follow-through exception in Law 13.4.2.
